passage: I'm Lavanya from the flat next door. I was visiting when Irfan's Ammi held out a spoon of mashed bitter gourd. Irfan, not yet two, pressed his lips shut and twisted his head away. A little got in anyway; he scrunched his nose, pushed it out with his tongue and shoved the bowl. Later, wet sand stuck to his palms at the park, and he held his hands out stiffly, whining, until they were wiped. I can't know what he thought, but he clearly wanted neither.

qa.q: What food did Irfan's Ammi offer him?
qa.a: She offered him a spoon of mashed bitter gourd.

qa.q: What did Irfan's scrunched nose and stiff hands suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They suggest he found the bitter taste and the wet, sticky sand unpleasant and wanted them gone.

qa.q: What small step could help Irfan get used to bitter gourd?
qa.a: His Ammi could put a tiny piece beside food he likes and let him touch or taste it without pressure, offering it again on other days.

qa.q: Why is Lavanya careful to say they can't know what Irfan thought?
qa.a: Lavanya is only watching from outside, so Lavanya can see his face and actions but can only guess at what was going on inside him.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler rejecting an unfamiliar bitter taste and an unpleasant texture, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday: Gautam put a spoon of plain curd near Nikita's lips. She gagged, spat it onto her bib and pushed his hand away.
Thursday: He left a small dab of curd at the edge of her plate beside the rice she loves. She poked it, licked her finger, grimaced, and went back to the rice.
The next Sunday: She dipped a rice ball into the curd herself, made a face at the first bite, then ate two more.

qa.q: What did Gautam put beside Nikita's rice on Thursday?
qa.a: He left a small dab of curd at the edge of her plate beside the rice.

qa.q: What does Nikita's gag on Monday show about how the curd felt to her?
qa.a: It shows the sour taste and cold texture were strange and unpleasant to her, so she rejected it straight away.

qa.q: Why did Gautam's slow approach work better than insisting on Monday?
qa.a: Leaving a little curd nearby let Nikita explore it at her own pace, next to food she already trusted, so the new taste became less of a shock. 👍

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt on Sunday watching her eat it?
qa.a: He might have felt pleased and relieved that his patience paid off, even though she still pulled a face at first.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting an unfamiliar taste and slowly accepting it over several days.

passage: The first cold morning in their Delhi flat, Sumit pulled a new woollen sweater over his son Naveen's head. Within seconds Naveen was squirming, tugging at the neck and whimpering. He scratched his arms, arched his back and finally flopped on the floor, crying and yanking the sleeves. Sumit knelt and ran his hand over the wool; it felt scratchy. He took it off, slipped a soft cotton vest on first, and put the sweater back over it. Naveen sniffed and toddled off to his blocks.

qa.q: What did Sumit put on Naveen under the sweater?
qa.a: He slipped a soft cotton vest on first and put the sweater back over it.

qa.q: Why was Naveen tugging and crying in the new sweater?
qa.a: The wool felt scratchy against his skin, and that uncomfortable feeling upset him enough that he wanted it off.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that a parent could copy?
qa.a: He checked the sweater himself to find the cause and changed the layer instead of scolding Naveen for fussing.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit had assumed Naveen was just being naughty?
qa.a: Naveen would probably keep crying and fighting the sweater, and the morning would turn into a struggle over something that really bothered him.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler rejecting an unpleasant sensory input, a scratchy fabric.

passage:
"Open wide, Darshan. It's pumpkin."
"No!" Darshan clamped his lips and turned his head.
"Just a tiny taste?" Harsha touched the spoon to his mouth.
He scrunched his nose, pushed out his tongue, and orange mush slid down his chin. "Yucky!"
"Okay, okay." Harsha wiped him. "Not today."
"Nana?"
"You want banana? Here." She put a slice beside the pumpkin on his plate. "The orange one can sit there too."

qa.q: What food did Harsha offer Darshan first?
qa.a: She offered him pumpkin.

qa.q: How can you tell Darshan felt disgust at the pumpkin?
qa.a: He clamped his lips, scrunched his nose, pushed out his tongue and said 'Yucky', which shows the taste or texture felt unpleasant to him.

qa.q: Which part of Harsha's approach might help Darshan accept new foods later?
qa.a: She stopped pushing and gave him a familiar banana, but left the pumpkin on the plate so he can see it again without pressure.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel when Darshan spits out food she cooked?
qa.a: She may feel a little tired or disappointed, but she stays patient and treats it as a normal toddler reaction.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler rejecting an unfamiliar taste with disgust cues, and a calm caregiver response.

passage:
Note for Ayesha's parents, from Deepika (playgroup)
Today we played with cold, wet oats in a tray. Ayesha poked it once, pulled her hand back and shook her fingers hard, making an 'eee' face. She wiped her hand on my kurta and would not go near the tray again. 😅
I gave her a spoon instead, and she scooped from a distance. We will try dry rice next time.

qa.q: What did the children play with in the tray?
qa.a: They played with cold, wet oats.

qa.q: What does Ayesha shaking her fingers and making an 'eee' face suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the slimy, wet feel was unpleasant to her and she wanted it off her skin.

qa.q: Which choice by Deepika helped, and why?
qa.a: Offering a spoon let Ayesha stay in the game without touching the texture she disliked, so she could explore at her own distance.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured that her dislike was noticed kindly and that the teacher has a gentle plan for next time.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting an unpleasant sensory input, recorded in a playgroup teacher's note.

passage: In the village near Margao, Sabina was feeding her niece Maria lunch on the balcao. Rice went down happily. Then came one piece of bitter gourd. Maria's face crumpled, her tongue pushed the piece out, and she shuddered all over, shaking her head so hard her curls bounced. "Too bitter?" Sabina laughed, wiping her chin. Maria clamped her lips shut and pushed the spoon away with both hands.

qa.q: What did Maria push out with her tongue?
qa.a: One piece of bitter gourd.

qa.q: What does Maria's shudder and shaking head suggest?
qa.a: She found the bitter taste disgusting and wanted nothing more of it.

qa.q: What could Sabina try next time she offers bitter gourd?
qa.a: Offer a tiny piece mixed with rice on another day, without forcing, so Maria can get used to the taste slowly.

qa.q: How does Sabina react to Maria's rejection?
qa.a: She laughs kindly and wipes her chin, taking it as a normal toddler reaction rather than being annoyed.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting a new bitter taste with her whole body.

passage: Bao carried his daughter Soo-ah down to the water at the beach in Melbourne. She loved the sand, until a strip of wet seaweed wrapped round her ankle. She stiffened, lifted her foot high, and screeched, "Eee! Off!", nose wrinkled, hands flapping. Bao peeled it away. Soo-ah refused to put that foot down again and pointed at the dry sand until he carried her back up the beach.

qa.q: What wrapped round Soo-ah's ankle?
qa.a: A strip of wet seaweed.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's wrinkled nose and screech suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was disgusted by the slimy seaweed and wanted it off her at once.

qa.q: How could Bao help Soo-ah feel okay near the water another time?
qa.a: Let her look at or poke seaweed with a stick from the dry sand first, and never push her towards it.

qa.q: What is it like for Bao when his plan for the water ends so fast?
qa.a: He may feel a little disappointed, but he accepts her reaction and carries her back.

grounding: Shows a toddler recoiling from an unpleasant slimy touch.

passage: I'm Mahima, and this summer I've been in charge of mango time with my baby brother Naveen. He loves the taste, but the juice running down his arms is another story. Yesterday he took two bites, looked at his sticky fingers, and held them out stiff, as far from his body as he could, making a "blech" face. When I wiped them he went straight back to the mango. Maybe it's the stickiness, not the fruit.

qa.q: What does Naveen love about mangoes?
qa.a: He loves the taste.

qa.q: What does Naveen's "blech" face suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He seemed disgusted by the sticky juice on his fingers, even though he enjoyed the mango itself.

qa.q: What could Mahima do to make mango time easier for Naveen?
qa.a: Cut the mango into small pieces or keep a cloth ready, so he can enjoy it without sticky hands.

qa.q: How does Mahima make sense of Naveen's reaction?
qa.a: Mahima guesses it is the stickiness, not the fruit, that bothers him, but can't be sure.

grounding: Shows a toddler rejecting an unpleasant sticky feeling while still enjoying the food, seen by an older sibling in summer.

passage:
First evening of Ramzan. At iftar, Leela Aunty from next door offers Wasim, twenty months, a slice of lime. He licks it, screws up his whole face, shudders, and spits. Everyone laughs.
A week later. Ammi offers him a new chutney on her fingertip. Wasim sniffs it, wrinkles his nose, and pushes her hand away.
On Eid. He watches Leela Aunty eat sheer khurma, reaches for her spoon, tastes it, and holds out his bowl.

qa.q: What did Leela Aunty offer Wasim on the first evening?
qa.a: A slice of lime.

qa.q: What did Wasim's screwed-up face and shudder show?
qa.a: Wasim felt strong disgust at the sour, unfamiliar taste.

qa.q: What seems to help Wasim accept a new food?
qa.a: Watching a trusted adult enjoy it and being allowed to try it himself, as with the sheer khurma.

qa.q: How might the adults feel when Wasim holds out his bowl?
qa.a: They would likely feel amused and pleased that he chose to try something new.

grounding: Over Ramzan and Eid, a toddler rejects sour and strong tastes but accepts a sweet one after watching an adult.

passage: After the first heavy rain, Pooja took Tarun, two, to the park near their Lucknow flat. He ran straight into the sandpit, now thick brown mud. Squelch. Tarun stopped, looked down at his sinking sandal, and pulled a loud "Eww!" face, lips drawn back, arms stiff at his sides. "Out! Out!" Pooja lifted him onto the grass and wiped his foot. Tarun inspected it, shuddered, and refused to go near the sandpit again.

qa.q: What had the sandpit turned into?
qa.a: Thick brown mud.

qa.q: What did Tarun's 'Eww!' face show?
qa.a: Tarun felt disgusted by the squelching mud on his foot.

qa.q: How did Pooja respond helpfully to Tarun's disgust?
qa.a: She lifted him out quickly, wiped his foot and let him avoid the sandpit, taking his feeling seriously.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel about Tarun's reaction?
qa.a: Pooja probably found it a bit funny but understood his discomfort and helped without teasing.

grounding: After the first monsoon rain, a toddler recoils in disgust from squelching mud.

passage:
"Tanu, try. Sarson ka saag. Only in winter!" Jatin held out a tiny spoon.
Tanuja, two, sniffed and turned her face. "No."
"Just a little?"
She licked it. Her tongue shot out. "Yuck! Yuck!" She wiped it on her sleeve.
"Too green?"
"Yuck."
"Okay. No more saag." Jatin broke off some makki roti. "This one's plain."
Tanuja examined it, bit, chewed. "Nice."
"Maybe saag another day."
"No saag," she said firmly.

qa.q: What dish did Jatin offer first?
qa.a: Sarson ka saag.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when her tongue shot out?
qa.a: Tanuja felt disgusted by the strong taste.

qa.q: How did Jatin handle Tanuja's refusal well?
qa.a: He accepted her 'yuck' without forcing, offered a plain food instead, and left room to try saag another day.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel hearing 'No saag' so firmly?
qa.a: Jatin probably felt amused and patient, knowing tastes can change later.

grounding: In winter, a toddler rejects a strong new taste and her father respects it while offering a plain alternative.

passage:
Playgroup note, summer.

At our mango picnic, Shalini, twenty months, tasted a slice of raw green mango. Her whole face crumpled. She stuck out her tongue, spat it out, and wiped her mouth with both hands, saying "Ew!"

We didn't force it. I gave her ripe mango instead, which she ate happily. I've told her parents she can try raw mango again another day, maybe with a little salt. — Vaibhav

qa.q: What did Shalini taste at the mango picnic?
qa.a: She tasted a slice of raw green mango.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel about the raw mango?
qa.a: Shalini was disgusted by the sour taste, crumpling her face and spitting it out.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav handle Shalini's reaction well?
qa.a: He did not force her, offered ripe mango instead, and suggested trying again later.

qa.q: How might Shalini's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would probably be amused and reassured that the teacher handled it gently.

grounding: A playgroup note records a toddler rejecting the sour taste of raw mango during a summer picnic.

passage:
Winter in the village near Ludhiana meant methi parathas every morning. Sonali tore a piece and put it in Irfan's mouth.

Irfan chewed once. His nose wrinkled. He pushed the paratha out with his tongue and scraped at it with his fingers, shaking his head.

"Bitter, na?" Sonali said, laughing. She wiped his mouth and gave him a piece of plain roti with ghee. Irfan chewed that one happily.

qa.q: What did Sonali give Irfan after the methi paratha?
qa.a: She gave him a piece of plain roti with ghee.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he pushed the paratha out?
qa.a: Irfan felt disgusted by the bitter taste, wrinkling his nose and shaking his head.

qa.q: How could Sonali help Irfan get used to new tastes over time?
qa.a: Offer a small bit of methi paratha again on other days, mixed with familiar food, without forcing it.

qa.q: How did Sonali see Irfan's reaction?
qa.a: Sonali found it funny and normal, laughing and offering something he liked.

grounding: During winter, a toddler rejects the bitter taste of methi paratha and his mother offers something familiar.

passage:
At Mid-Autumn Festival in Shanghai, Amara was minding Chen while his parents set up lanterns in the courtyard.

A neighbour gave Chen a piece of mooncake with a salted egg yolk inside. He bit it, froze, and spat it onto the ground. He wiped his tongue with his sleeve and made a loud "Bleh!"

Amara laughed and gave him a slice of pear. Chen took it and checked it carefully before biting.

qa.q: What was inside the mooncake?
qa.a: There was a salted egg yolk inside.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when he wiped his tongue with his sleeve?
qa.a: Chen felt disgusted by the unfamiliar salty taste.

qa.q: How did Amara help Chen after he spat out the mooncake?
qa.a: She stayed calm and gave him a familiar food, a slice of pear.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel about Chen spitting out the mooncake?
qa.a: The neighbour might feel slightly embarrassed or amused, knowing small children often dislike new tastes.

grounding: At the Mid-Autumn Festival, a toddler rejects an unfamiliar salty taste in a mooncake.

passage: I'm Chinmay from the flat next door, and I was there when Asif's Ammi gave him his first bite of bitter gourd. He chewed once, stopped, and his whole face wrinkled. He pushed the mush out with his tongue and shoved the spoon away. His sister Rubina giggled. "Same, Asif, same." His Ammi offered it again. He clamped his lips and shook his head hard. I can't say what it tasted like to him, but I've never seen a face like that.

qa.a: She gave him his first bite of bitter gourd.

qa.q: What did Asif's wrinkled face and clamped lips suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he felt disgusted by the bitter taste and didn't want any more of it.
